Story: Every Qloo call goes through one client
Description: One client in cue/qloo/ is the only code allowed to talk to Qloo. It sends the key to the hackathon server, times out after 10 seconds, and emits a trace event for every call. Anything that skips it would also skip the cache, the rate limiter and the trace panel, so this blocks every other story.
Acceptance: A real Search call works with the hackathon key and emits one qloo_call event with endpoint, params, time and cache state.

Story: Reject parameters Qloo would silently ignore
Description: Qloo quietly ignores a parameter that doesn't fit the filter.type, so a bad request returns wrong results with no error. The param checker compares every request with Qloo's Entity Type Parameter Guide and refuses it before it leaves, with a reason and a hint (for example, use urn:entity:videogame).
Acceptance: filter.release_year.min on an artist query is rejected without reaching Qloo; every type we query accepts filter.popularity.max.

Story: Serve repeat calls from the cache, never from the repo
Description: Name-to-ID lookups are kept for 30 days and other answers for 24 hours, keyed by endpoint and sorted parameters. Failed calls are never cached. Qloo allows private server-side caching but not Qloo data in a public repo, so the cache stays on the server.
Acceptance: A repeated Insights call returns in about 0 ms with no request sent; a failed call leaves nothing in the cache.

Story: Survive rate limits and Qloo errors
Description: A token bucket keeps us under Qloo's limit. 429s, server errors and network errors retry up to three times with growing waits and respect Retry-After; other 4xx errors fail at once, because retrying a bad request never fixes it.
Acceptance: Tests show a 429 followed by success, giving up after the limit, and no retry on a 400.

Story: Run the demo with no outside calls
Description: DEMO_MODE=true serves every Qloo answer from the cache and fails loudly on a miss, so a recording or a judging session can't die on a rate limit. The Qloo client side is built; the full run still needs checking end to end with the model cache.
Acceptance: With DEMO_MODE on and a warm cache, a full artist run and a full supervisor run finish with zero network calls.

Story: Nine Qloo tools with the agreed signatures
Description: One module per Qloo endpoint in cue/tools/, all going through the Qloo client and picking it up from the run's context. Insights always asks for explainability and carries each item's rank, because raw affinity barely varies.
Acceptance: Every tool ran live once with no errors; tests use fake values only.

Story: Find an entity only by its exact name
Description: Search's first hit is often a wrong near-match (Aditi Ramesh came back as Ramesh). find_entity keeps only exact matches after ignoring case, accents, punctuation and a leading 'the', checks other spellings, and for musicians searches artist entries only.
Acceptance: A name Qloo doesn't have returns not found, never the nearest fuzzy hit.

Story: Merge the entries that belong to one person
Description: One human can be an artist, a person and an author entry in Qloo. Results that share a Spotify or MusicBrainz ID merge into one, with the artist entry as the signal, because person entries give different matches and empty demographics.
Acceptance: Prateek Kuhad's artist and person entries come back as one result.

Story: Find an artist from their Spotify link
Description: Route 1, the happy path. The artist pastes their Spotify artist link and Cue looks the ID up in Qloo. Singers, bands and composers who release music are usually found this way, with no guessing.
Acceptance: A Spotify link Qloo knows resolves to one artist entry with no other questions; the trace says 'found via Spotify'.

Story: Find lyricists through MusicBrainz
Description: Route 2. Lyricists are usually person entries in Qloo with no Spotify ID, but they carry a MusicBrainz ID. Cue turns the Spotify link into an MBID with find_mbid_by_spotify (already in cue/identity/musicbrainz.py, through shared_client() so the 1 request per second limit is shared), then looks the MBID up in Qloo. The direct lookup missed 2 of 3 lyricists in testing, so the backup is a MusicBrainz name search that must match their Spotify link.
Acceptance: Amitabh Bhattacharya, Irshad Kamil and Swanand Kirkire each resolve to their Qloo entry from a Spotify link.

Story: Match an artist Qloo doesn't know yet
Description: Route 3. A short profile (artists you sound like, genre, five favourite songs, followers, previous work, career goal) becomes a taste stand-in: the agent names look-alike artists and genre tags, and each must be found in Qloo by exact name or it is dropped. The command line already accepts --sounds-like; the profile questions and the agent's suggestions are still to wire into the site.
Acceptance: An unknown artist with at least one resolvable look-alike gets matches labelled 'based on artists you resemble'; with none, the run says there isn't enough data.

Story: Confirm 'Is this you?' and remember the answer
Description: Whichever route finds the artist, show a card with name, image, short description and listener count. On confirm, save the user-to-Qloo-ID link in Supabase so they're never asked again. The saved link holds IDs we chose, not Qloo response data.
Acceptance: A confirmed artist goes straight to results on their next visit.

Story: Pick the right artist when names collide
Description: Without a Spotify link, search by name and role (artist entries for singers and composers, person then author entries for lyricists), narrow by the genre and country they gave, and show up to three cards plus 'None of these is me', which goes to Route 3. A name search for 'Divine' found a different artist from the Mumbai rapper.
Acceptance: Two artists with the same name never merge, and the user can always reach Route 3.

Story: Show which onboarding route was used
Description: The trace panel says 'found via Spotify', 'found via MusicBrainz' or 'matched as a mix of similar artists', so judges can see the agent working around gaps in Qloo's data.
Acceptance: Every run's trace starts with the route that resolved the artist.

Story: The planner decides what to look up
Description: A small model reads the brief and decides the production types, sections and brief tags; code builds the actual Qloo calls. It gets a second round after seeing a summary of the first, and leaves out types a brief rules out (no shooting games for a monsoon romance).
Acceptance: Planner decisions appear in the trace as step=planner with a note; an injection attempt in an artist name doesn't change the plan.

Story: Independent Qloo calls run at the same time
Description: The executor runs calls in dependency order and independent ones in parallel, with a 20-second timeout each. A failed call marks its part of the run as not enough data instead of crashing it.
Acceptance: The production calls start together in the trace, and a timeout doesn't stop the run.

Story: Match productions in three popularity sections
Description: Productions are split into big screen (popularity 0.90 and above), prime time (0.70 to 0.90) and indie gems (below 0.70), each its own Insights call, so one hugely popular show can't crowd out realistic placements for an indie artist.
Acceptance: Every section Qloo has data for shows its own matches.

Story: Rank by what this artist's fans like more than similar artists' fans
Description: Raw results put the same popular shows (Aarya, Criminal Justice) at the top for every Indian artist. Lift fixes that: the same query runs for four similar artists, and each production is scored by how much more this artist's fans like it. Inside a section, match = 0.70 x lift rank + 0.30 x audience fit.
Acceptance: Lift and its inputs appear in FitScore.inputs for every ranked production, or it is marked insufficient_data.

Story: Scores come from code, never from the model
Description: The fit score is a pure function of Qloo's numbers. The writer's output has no score field; scores are joined in by code afterwards.
Acceptance: The same inputs always give the same score, covered by unit tests.

Story: Never show a made-up name
Description: The grounding guard removes any show, film, game, brand or artist from the writer's text that isn't a Qloo entity returned earlier in the run, and logs it as a guard_drop.
Acceptance: A planted made-up show name is removed and logged.

Story: Never claim a placement that didn't happen
Description: Pitch text may not say a song was used somewhere unless our data shows it. The writer also may not state anything about a production's plot, setting or mood; it may only imagine a scene the music could suit. A live run had invented a 'monsoon setting' for Ved.
Acceptance: A planted 'your song was featured in' sentence is removed, and an empty reason is replaced by a sentence built from the facts.

Story: Keep explicit titles out of pitches
Description: Qloo returned an adult podcast in a live run. The content filter drops candidates with explicit words in their titles before scoring. It checks titles only; a tag-based check would be stronger.
Acceptance: No candidate with an explicit title reaches the writer.

Story: Get a pitch email for each production
Description: The writer turns scored, checked matches into a pitch kit: a reason and a subject and body per production, three per section. Artists are they/their, and no gender is guessed. Pitches are drafts; Cue never sends anything.
Acceptance: A live run for Prateek Kuhad scored 109 matches and wrote 9 pitches in about 28 seconds for under a cent of Claude.

Story: A writer failure still returns the matches
Description: If the writer fails, the run returns its scored matches with no text and a guard_drop saying why, instead of an error page.
Acceptance: A forced writer error still produces ranked matches.

Story: Every paid model call stays inside a budget
Description: All model calls go through cue/agents/common/llm.py, which caches by PROMPT_VERSION and refuses any call that could pass LLM_BUDGET_USD. With no budget set, no paid call is made.
Acceptance: A run with LLM_BUDGET_USD unset makes no paid call; each run reports its Claude cost.

Story: Build the fan profile from the artist's own tags
Description: Qloo's urn:tag results put place and brand tags first (VISA, Mocktails), so the profile uses the artist entry's own tags (43 clean music, mood, theme and audience tags for Prateek Kuhad), plus the fans' age and gender lean.
Acceptance: The profile shows music and audience tags and an age and gender lean, each traced to a Qloo call.

Story: Run either mode from the command line
Description: python -m cue.run artist|supervisor runs a full run with a brief, sounds-like artists, a production type, pitch emails, the trace and a JSON file in the shape the website will receive. It's how the team checks demo picks before the site exists.
Acceptance: Both example commands in the README run end to end and print their cost.

Story: A supervisor gets a shortlist of under-the-radar artists
Description: Same pipeline in reverse: from a show, film, game or brand, find the artists its audience likes, capped at popularity 0.80, scored by lift against four similar productions' audiences, and written up as a brief with a Spotify link per artist.
Acceptance: Bandish Bandits returned 8 shortlisted artists, all at or under the cap, in about 26 seconds.

Story: Widen the cap when too few artists come back
Description: If fewer than 8 artists come back under 0.80, the cap widens to 0.85 and the trace says so.
Acceptance: A step=widen event appears whenever the cap was widened.

Story: Drop artists who have died or disbanded
Description: Qloo has no birth, death or debut dates, so the cap returned Bhimsen Joshi and Mehdi Hassan. The top 12 get a MusicBrainz life-span check; ended artists are dropped, and artists with no answer are kept and marked unverified.
Acceptance: For Bandish Bandits, Bhimsen Joshi, Mehdi Hassan, Meet Bros Anjjan and Rashid Khan are dropped.

Story: Treat honorific spellings as one artist
Description: 'Ustad Rashid Khan' and 'Rashid Khan' are one person. Supervisor mode ignores leading titles such as Ustad, Pandit and Shri when merging, and finds a missing MBID by a strict MusicBrainz name search.
Acceptance: Shiv Kumar Sharma and Ustad Rashid Khan are found and dropped as ended.

Story: Never call the shortlist new or emerging
Description: Popularity alone can't tell a newcomer from a veteran, so the shortlist is labelled 'Under-the-radar artists' and the writer is told never to say new, emerging, up-and-coming or rising.
Acceptance: No shortlist text uses those words; the result event carries SHORTLIST_LABEL.

Story: Start a run and stream its steps
Description: POST /runs starts an artist or supervisor run (run_artist and run_supervisor are the entry points) and returns a run ID; GET /runs/{id}/events streams every step and Qloo call over server-sent events; GET /runs/{id} returns the final pitch kit or brief. The API keeps no state between requests except the cache.
Acceptance: A run started from curl streams planner, Qloo and result events in order and ends with the pitch kit.

Story: Save runs and results
Description: Runs, matches, fit scores, pitch kits, briefs and the user-to-Qloo-ID links go in Supabase. Raw Qloo responses never do.
Acceptance: A finished run can be reopened from its ID after the API restarts.

Story: Artist mode on the website
Description: Onboarding, then results grouped by section (big screen, prime time, indie gems), each card with name, type, fit score, Qloo's reason and a pitch email with a copy button. No trend is shown, because Qloo's trending data is frozen.
Acceptance: An artist goes from a Spotify link to copyable pitch emails without leaving the page.

Story: Supervisor mode on the website
Description: A production goes in; the shortlist comes out under the SHORTLIST_LABEL heading, with a Listen link per artist from spotify_url and an 'unverified' note when the life-span check had no answer.
Acceptance: A supervisor gets the Bandish Bandits shortlist with working Listen links.

Story: Watch every Qloo call live
Description: A trace panel beside the results fills from the run's event stream: each Qloo call with endpoint, key parameters, time and a cache hit or miss chip, planner notes, guard drops highlighted, and parallel calls shown starting together, under a count of 'N Qloo calls across M endpoints'. This is how judges see how deeply Cue uses Qloo.
Acceptance: Every qloo_call event in a run appears in the panel as it happens.

Story: Open on a real example
Description: The first view shows a pre-warmed run, clearly marked as an example, so a judge sees what Cue does before typing anything.
Acceptance: The home page shows a finished example run with no wait.

Story: Works on a phone
Description: Both modes and the trace panel stay usable at phone width.
Acceptance: No sideways scrolling at 400 px wide.

Story: A live health box from the guards
Description: Show numbers the code already produces on real runs: made-up names caught, placement claims caught, not-enough-data rate, onboarding route, run time and cache hit rate. No extra model calls.
Acceptance: The eval page shows these counts from recent real runs.

Story: Results start showing within seconds
Description: Live runs take about 26 to 30 seconds on a cold cache, so the page streams steps and matches as they arrive instead of waiting for the whole run (PRD NF-1 and NF-2).
Acceptance: First events show within 5 seconds, a full run finishes within 60, and a cached demo run within 5.

Story: Collect about 300 known placements
Description: Real cases of an artist whose song was used in a show, film, game or ad, each with a note of where we learned it. Only sources whose terms allow it (PRD Q-4). No Qloo data in the file.
Acceptance: evalsets/placements.jsonl has about 300 rows, each with a source.

Story: Fix the practice and test split
Description: 60 rows for practice and tuning, 240 for the final test, fixed once, so nobody tunes the score on the test set.
Acceptance: The split is stored in the file and never changes after the first full run.

Story: Run Claude alone, Claude with search, and Cue on the same set
Description: System A is Claude Opus 5.5 with no tools, B adds web search, C is Cue. The same model throughout means Qloo is the only difference. Runs offline, never against the live demo, so it can't use up the Qloo quota judges depend on. Vedant hooks Cue in as system C.
Acceptance: All three systems answer every practice-set row and results land in eval/results.json with our scores only.

Story: Score hit rate in the top 10
Description: Is the known artist in the system's top 10 for the show, and the known show in its top 10 for the artist? Both directions.
Acceptance: Hit rate is reported per system and per direction.

Story: Score made-up names
Description: Every name a system suggests is looked up with Qloo search; the share that doesn't resolve is its made-up rate. Cue's grounding guard should make it zero.
Acceptance: Made-up rate is reported per system.

Story: Score the under-the-radar share
Description: The share of suggested artists under the popularity cap. Plain models tend to suggest famous names, which are useless for indie artists.
Acceptance: Under-the-radar share is reported per system.

Story: Score consistency on a small subset
Description: Run the same input three times and measure how much the top 10s overlap. On 30 rows only, to keep cost down.
Acceptance: Consistency is reported per system from 30 rows.

Story: Report time and cost per run
Description: Median and slowest run time and Claude cost per system, from real API calls.
Acceptance: Time and cost appear in the results for every system.

Story: Keep the eval cheap
Description: Cue's eval skips the writer (scores are decided before any text), every answer is cached, the practice set runs first so the real bill is known, baselines may use batch processing, and answers are short lists.
Acceptance: The practice-set run's cost is known before the full set is started.

Story: Check every push with a small eval
Description: A GitHub Actions job runs a 30-row eval of Cue on every push and fails if its hit rate drops more than 5 points.
Acceptance: A push that breaks matching fails the check.

Story: Publish an eval page
Description: A table of all three systems on each score, one chart for hit rate, 3 or 4 side-by-side examples, and how the eval works in plain words. Honest even where Cue doesn't win.
Acceptance: The eval page shows A, B and C on the same test set, generated from eval/results.json.

Story: The demo is live and stays live
Description: API on Cloud Run with at least one instance during judging so there's no cold start, website on Vercel, cache on Upstash Redis, keys and LLM_BUDGET_USD in Secret Manager, and a health check.
Acceptance: The live site works from a fresh browser with no login, and stays up from submission to 16 Nov.

Story: Warm the cache for the demo
Description: Run the demo artists and shows ahead of time so judges get instant results.
Acceptance: Demo runs come back from cache in under 5 seconds.

Story: Pick demo artists that work
Description: Choose the demo artists and shows by running them through python -m cue.run with --emails --trace, using artist entries rather than person entries.
Acceptance: Every demo pick produces sensible matches and pitches with no guard drops worth hiding.

Story: Write the Devpost description
Description: The problem in plain words, who it's for, how it works, a table of every Qloo endpoint and the step it powers, lift explained ('your fans over-index on X compared with fans of similar artists'), the eval results, and what we don't claim (no trend because Qloo's data is static, under-the-radar not emerging). Judges may score from the write-up alone.
Acceptance: The write-up names every Qloo endpoint Cue uses and links the live demo and repo.

Story: Screenshots of both modes and the trace
Description: Images of artist results, the supervisor shortlist and the trace panel for the Devpost page.
Acceptance: At least one screenshot each of artist mode, supervisor mode and the trace panel.

Story: Submit with every requirement met
Description: Run the COMPETITION.md checklist: live demo link, public repo with setup steps, MIT license showing in the repo's About section, text description, new project not entered elsewhere. Submit by 30 Oct, 6 PM ET.
Acceptance: Every box in COMPETITION.md section 3 is ticked and the entry is submitted before 6 PM ET on 30 Oct.

Story: Show where fans cluster in a city
Description: Optional. The heatmap needs an area and only returns small map squares, so it can show which neighbourhoods of a chosen city an artist's fans cluster in (Worli, Lower Parel, Bandra for Prateek Kuhad in Mumbai), for gig and local ad ideas. It can't rank cities. First to cut.
Acceptance: For a chosen city, the artist sees the top neighbourhoods; the main run isn't slowed.
